localeVisibleInspection.en: Actually read all six English stems and all 24 English option texts. The mathematical conditions, quantities, qualifiers, table rows and option assertions are identical to Chinese; computations below apply independently to those same explicit conditions.

task_fidelity.evidence: Preserves the source H2-versus-N2 thermal-motion comparison. The visible common-temperature equilibrium condition states the statistical model rather than asserting all individual speeds. Equal mean kinetic energy is a directly relevant inference, not a different source task replacing speed comparison.

redundancy.evidence: A is energy equality, B is an every-particle quantifier, and C/D are opposite rms-speed comparisons. These are four distinct predicates, not repeated equal quantities or a combination code. Both A and C require independent selection in native multiple mode.

answer_leakage.evidence: Neither species' speed nor mean energy is given in the stem. Atmospheric species, temperature and model are conditions. Other package questions contain no species-speed comparison or keyed response to this item.

mathematics.independent_solution: For the visible classical equilibrium model, mean translational kinetic energy is 3kT/2 and v_rms=sqrt(3kT/m). Thus A and C hold, with H2/N2 rms ratio approximately sqrt(28/2)=sqrt(14). Speed distributions overlap; B is false. This is a characteristic-speed model, not a claim about all individual molecules.

option_checks.evidence: Same T gives 3kT/2 for both molecular species. Energy equality is not equivalent to equal speed or to C; no incorrect procedure is needed for this true assertion.

Independent counterexample: a slow H2 molecule and a faster N2 molecule are both allowed by overlapping classical equilibrium speed distributions. Reproduced mistake: replace the inequality of rms averages by an inequality for every pair of particles. This universal assertion is stronger than, not equivalent to, C.
v_rms varies as m^(-1/2); m_H2<m_N2, so H2 has greater rms speed. Distinct from A and opposite to D; no misconception applies to the true inequality.

Independent mass comparison yields the reverse inequality. Reproduced mistaken procedure: use v_rms proportional to sqrt(m) instead of 1/sqrt(m), giving v_N2/v_H2=sqrt(14). D is the opposite assertion to C, not an equivalent spelling.

The explicit Figure 24 process definitions match original n17; Figure 30 still requires its V-T arrows. redundancy.evidence: One coherent five-row response follows the original two-figure energy comparison. A changes three rows, C two, D three relative to the true table. No table is equivalent to another, and rows are not fragmented into five yes/no clicks.

answer_leakage.evidence: The stated isobaric and isothermal processes are necessary original definitions, not author answers. U(T) and the energy-change table are not printed. Shared thermal concepts elsewhere do not state these five directed answers. Table shape and detail are comparable for A-D.

mathematics.independent_solution: Under the visible fixed-composition ideal-gas equilibrium model, U follows T. Figure 24: constant-p heating increases U; isothermal compression leaves U unchanged. Figure 30: rightward 1-to-2 increases T, vertical 2-to-3 keeps T fixed, leftward 3-to-1 decreases T. Ordered results are increase, unchanged, increase, unchanged, decrease, exactly table B. No schematic pixel ratio is used.

option_checks.evidence: A wrongly decreases U in both isothermal compressions and leaves U fixed in 3-to-1 cooling. Reproduced procedure: make U depend on V alone; V rises, falls, rises, falls, stays fixed in the five rows. That exactly generates A. Its complete row vector differs from B/C/D.
All five rows individually agree with U(T): +,0,+,0,-. B is the only complete table matching this vector; no false-rule reproduction applies.

C adds U during 1'-to-2 and 2-to-3 although both are isothermal. Reproduced procedure: use actual T direction on non-isothermal paths but assert every compression raises U, including fixed-T compression. This gives +,+,+,+,-. It is not equivalent to B or the pressure-only table D.

Reproduced procedure: assume U depends on p alone. Figure 24 p is constant then increases; Figure 30 line through origin is isobaric, vertical compression increases p, fixed-V cooling decreases p. Thus 0,+,0,+,-, exactly D, whereas actual U follows T. Distinct from all other row vectors.

task_fidelity.evidence: Preserves 50 m^3 air, 200 cm^3 liquid water, standard pressure, 20 C and the comparison of molecular totals. Visible water density, molar mass and temperature offset make the source's material assumptions explicit. The ratio adds a coherent quantitative comparison; the answer is not a volume copy.

redundancy.evidence: Each option gives both a ratio defined as air/water and its consistent greater-count conclusion. Ratios 0.0053, 250000, 0.19 and 187 are distinct, not equivalent forms; no separate count-cell clicks.

answer_leakage.evidence: Stem provides material constants but no molecule count or ratio. All four alternatives use the same comparison form, and the vacuum item supplies no computed air/water ratio.

mathematics.independent_solution: For the visible constants, n_air=101325*50/(8.314*293.15)=2078.67 mol; n_water=1000*(200e-6)/0.018=11.1111 mol. N_A cancels, so r=n_air/n_water=187.080795, approximately 187; room air contains more molecules. This numerical result is conditional on the explicitly chosen density and gas model, unlike the original's implicit material approximations.

option_checks.evidence: r is defined air/water, not water/air. Reproduced inversion gives 1/187.080795=0.00534528 and the consequent wrong greater-count direction, matching A. Not equivalent to D under the defined numerator.

Reproduced wrong model: treat liquid water as the same ideal gas at the same p and T as room air, cancel p/(RT), and divide 50 by 200e-6. This gives 250000, exactly B. Liquid water requires mass/molar mass, so B is false and not a rounding of D.

Reproduced thousandfold unit error: treat 200 g water as 200 kg while using M=0.018 kg/mol. Then n_water is 1000 times too large and r=0.1870808, approximately 0.19, with the wrong comparison direction. C is not equivalent to 0.0053 or 187.
The independent SI-volume and density calculation gives r approximately 187 and hence air greater. N_A cancels from the ratio; D is uniquely true at the shown precision. No misconception applies.

redundancy.evidence: 0.48, 0.96, 0.97 and 8.11 percent are distinct at their displayed two-decimal percentage precision. The close 0.96/0.97 pair tests final versus initial normalization, not duplicate spellings; correct rounding of 0.9672739 percent is 0.97 percent.

answer_leakage.evidence: Definition and units settle which source quantity is asked, but no percentage or T-proportionality equation is given. Options have identical phrasing. Molecular-motion item uses rms speed in a different common-T species comparison and does not give this heating percentage.

mathematics.independent_solution: For the visible source-defined overline(v^2), the classical mean translational energy is proportional to T. Initial and final T are 310.15 and 313.15 K. Relative-to-initial increase is 100*3/310.15=0.9672739 percent, rounded to 0.97 percent: only C. Preserve this conditional kinetic model and original definition separately from rms speed.

option_checks.evidence: Reproduced quantity substitution: compute 100*(sqrt(313.15/310.15)-1)=0.482473 percent, rounded 0.48 percent. This is rms-speed heating, not the visible overline(v^2). A is not equivalent to C.

Reproduced denominator error: divide the change by final T, not initial T, yielding 100*3/313.15=0.958006 percent, rounded 0.96 percent. The correct initial-normalized result rounds to 0.97, not 0.96 at the stated precision. Distinct numerical claims; neither a silent tolerance nor truncation is introduced.
310.15-to-313.15 K gives initial-normalized 0.9672739 percent, which rounds to 0.97 percent. C alone is true at the displayed precision, with no incorrect procedure required.
Reproduced Celsius-ratio error: 100*(40-37)/37=8.108108 percent, rounded 8.11 percent. Thermal proportionality requires absolute T; D is not equivalent to the kelvin result.

task_fidelity.evidence: Preserves source SI pressure 1.3e-10 Pa, 27 C and 1 cm^3, asking a residual-gas molecule count. The mmHg value remains approximate and the visible instruction correctly chooses the stated SI datum, rather than silently treating both approximate values as exact.

redundancy.evidence: Each alternative is a full molecular count with comparable notation. Counts differ by identifiable temperature or volume conversion errors, and no alternative is another notation for 3.1e4.

answer_leakage.evidence: k_B, SI pressure and temperature offset are data; pV/(k_B T) or its resulting count is not given. The air/water item has different volumes and no absolute molecular count, so it does not directly supply this result.

mathematics.independent_solution: N=pV/(k_B T), with p=1.3e-10 Pa, V=1e-6 m^3, T=300.15 K, gives N=31370.5203, approximately 3.1e4 molecules at the option precision. The mmHg statement is approximate, not a replacement exact pressure.

option_checks.evidence: The SI calculation gives 3.137052e4 molecules, rounded 3.1e4. A is the unique correct count, not a density or mole count; no misconception applies.
Reproduced Celsius error: use T=27 in pV/(k_B T), giving 348735.14 molecules, approximately 3.5e5. B is distinct from A and is false because 27 C is 300.15 K.

Reproduced cubing error: convert 1 cm^3 to 1e-2 m^3 by applying only the linear cm-to-m factor, instead of (1e-2)^3. The result is 10000 times A, 3.137052e8, approximately 3.1e8. Not equivalent to any other option.
Reproduced omitted conversion: use V=1 m^3, producing 1000000 times A, 3.137052e10, approximately 3.1e10. This does not count the stated 1 cm^3 and is distinct from C's linear-factor error.

task_fidelity.evidence: Preserves 4 mol monoatomic ideal gas, 500 J compression and adiabatic temperature-rise task. Explicit net work on the gas, closed-system and negligible bulk energy changes define the textbook first-law model rather than guessing compressor gross energy or changing work direction. Full temperature-change recognition retains energy balance, sign and heat-capacity distinctions.

redundancy.evidence: A uses wrong heat capacity, B wrong work sign, C the computed rise and D zero change. These are four distinct complete signed temperature changes, not unit-converted duplicates.

answer_leakage.evidence: The source's necessary positive-on-gas sign clarification can rule out cooling qualitatively but does not disclose the numerical rise or monoatomic heat capacity. Every option has comparable mathematical form; no other package item supplies this gas's energy balance.

mathematics.independent_solution: For the explicit visible net-work model, Q=0 and Delta U=Q+W_on=500 J. Monoatomic C_V=(3/2)nR, so Delta T=500/(1.5*4*8.314)=10.023254 K, approximately +10.0 K. This uses net gas work; it is not a conclusion about unknown compressor gross losses.

option_checks.evidence: Reproduced heat-capacity substitution: use C_p=(5/2)nR instead of C_V=(3/2)nR in Delta U, giving 500/(2.5*4*8.314)=6.013952 K, approximately +6.0 K. A is not equivalent to the constant-volume internal-energy slope needed here.

Reproduced sign error: insert +500 J as W_by in Delta U=Q-W_by rather than the explicit W_on, giving -500/(1.5*4*8.314) approximately -10.0 K. The visible positive-on-gas condition makes B false, not equivalent to C.
Net +500 J goes into U; dividing by (3/2)*4*8.314 J/K gives +10.023254 K, rounded +10.0 K. No temperature-offset conversion applies to a difference; C is uniquely true.
Reproduced adiabatic/isothermal confusion: take Q=0 to mean Delta T=0 and omit W_on from the first law. Actual Delta U=500 J, so D is false and distinct from A/B/C.
